piezas.titular: Grading a text prepared with AI requires a sample of the student’s own writing
piezas.entradilla: Asking students to explain how they used artificial intelligence makes sense if they know the rules before they start. Giving a mark takes something more, even when the declaration is entirely sincere.
cuerpo: In an English class, the task might be to write to a hotel to get a forgotten jacket back. One student can explain what happened, but looks up how to politely ask for the item to be sent on. Another writes the whole request in Spanish and hands in a flawless machine translation. Both tick the AI-use box. If the mark is meant to say how well each of them manages in English, what do we do with those two emails?

There is a good argument for having both emails written in full in class, without AI. The task takes little time, the conditions are known, and when marking it you can point out precisely what each student needs to practise. It is also a question of fairness. If one student is required to find her own words, she has a right to expect the same standard to be applied to the work of the student at the next desk. To find out whether someone can write an email without assistance, asking them to write it that way seems to me the most reasonable test.

The [report by the Office for Students and Advance HE on English higher education](https://www.officeforstudents.org.uk/publications/making-ai-work-for-students-reflections-on-institutional-practice/) lends weight to that argument. It warns that many unsupervised tasks can be completed well with AI without demonstrating the mastery they were meant to assess. It recommends turning to controlled-conditions tests when that certainty is needed, as the paper reported when it looked at [assessment without AI](pieza:2026-11-12/ofs-evaluacion-sin-ia). The problem arises when that solution becomes the only way of assessing. Learning to review an email also deserves class time. Noticing that the translation demands an urgent delivery from the hotel that nobody meant to request is an achievement that deserves recognition.

That is why I would set aside part of the work for each student to show the skill for which they receive the mark. The rest can allow help where it serves the purpose of the exercise. In the hotel case, the brief could allow the first email to be prepared at home with notes, a dictionary or even a translator that proposes the whole text. When handing in the text, it would be enough to point to one expression that was hard to work out, explain what help was used, if any, and why that wording was chosen. Spain’s National Institute of Educational Technologies and Teacher Training (INTEF) offers a [model declaration of AI use (PDF, in Spanish)](https://code.intef.es/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ANEXO-2-Modelo-de-declaraci%C3%B3n-Uso-de-la-IA-.pdf). The value of [declaring the help received](pieza:2026-11-15/declarar-uso-ia-transparencia) also depends on what teachers then do with that information.

If consulting a polite formula was allowed, acknowledging the consultation should never lower the mark. Deducting points in that case would favour the student who, having made the same consultation, chose to keep quiet about it. Nor would it be fair to assume that writing a request has been mastered because the second student has frankly explained that she translated the whole email. Her declaration settles a doubt about where the text came from. What she could write by herself remains to be found out.

The hotel’s reply could serve for that. On Monday, the teacher can write on the board that reception has found two jackets and needs to know which one to return. The whole class has a few minutes to reply individually, with each student’s usual supports and without machine translation. From day one, the brief should specify that the first part will be assessed on the revision of the email. In the second, what will count is whether the description makes it possible to recognise the garment and whether the tone is suitable for asking for it to be returned. That way the revision work done at home is kept, and a writing sample is obtained that can be marked in a few lines.

When marking, it may turn out that the colour and the torn pocket identify the jacket perfectly, but that the last sentence sounds like an order. The next task can start right there. It is enough to underline that sentence and ask the student to try two more courteous ways of asking for the return.
